title: What we now know about the UK economy in four charts
text:
The UK may have no involvement in the US-Iran war, but the country is feeling the full force of the conflict on its economy.

Soaring energy prices are set to dent growth in the short term, push up inflation and leave living standards in a "grim" place, according to the latest official forecast from the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).

Interest rates are also predicted to rise, making borrowing more expensive, along with government debt repayments.

Chancellor John Healey warned the nation faces "real challenges ahead" as he announced policies that he said would offer "breathing space" for households in the coming months.

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you

"What we face today are global economic storms," he said. "We can't wish them away. We must choose the course we steer through them."

In its first assessment of the UK economy since the Middle East conflict started, the OBR said rising energy prices were the biggest risk to the economy in the near future.

Despite raising its growth forecast for this year, it sharply cut its prediction for next year from 1.6% to 1%.

Growth is then set to rebound in the following years.

When an economy grows, businesses tend to invest more, create more jobs and give pay rises to workers, which leaves people feeling better off on average, though it can take time and not everyone necessarily benefits.

Companies making higher profits also pay more in tax, which can enable the government to spend more on public services. When there is slow economic growth, or the economy shrinks, the opposite can occur.

Inflation can weigh on growth and the OBR has forecast that prices are set to rise at a faster pace as higher energy bills filter through supply chains and to consumers, especially in 2027.

High global oil prices have already hit drivers at the pumps, with petrol priced at almost £1.73 per litre on average, while diesel is near £1.99.

Elevated oil prices over time can lead to prices edging upwards across a host of goods, such as food, as companies pass on the higher expenses they face to consumers.

Goods are typically transported to destinations by lorries and vans, so high fuel prices can have far-reaching consequences.

The OBR now thinks inflation will stay higher for longer than previously forecast, peaking at 3.8% in 2027.

Despite the cost-of-living support announced by the government, economists at Pantheon Macroeconomics said the measures were "small beer given the surge in inflation we expect over the winter".

High inflation paints a bleak picture when it comes to living standards and the OBR has forecast a dip next year as energy bills hit the spending power of households.

Those on lower incomes are set to be hit harder, however, because energy costs eat up a bigger share of their monthly budget and disposable income.

Real household disposable income, a measure of living standards, is forecast to grow from 2027, but not by as much as previously thought.

"It's a pretty grim picture," according to the OBR's David Miles, who says there has been "virtually no growth" for individuals since before the Covid pandemic.

"It's been a dismal period in British economic history."

What the Budget offers for under 25s - and what it leaves out

Inflation is expected to average 3.4% next year, before falling to the Bank of England's 2% target towards the end of the decade.

The Bank is widely expected to raise interest rates next week due to higher inflation in recent months. Rates are currently at 3.75%, but the OBR now forecasts they could rise to as high as 4.5% in the coming years.

It had previously forecast two interest rate cuts this year.

Higher rates makes borrowing money more expensive but can boost returns on savings.

Inflation also raises the cost of borrowing for the government, with spending on debt interest set to rise.

Such repayments are also predicted to increase the overall amount the government borrows, which is set to increase every year by more than had been previously forecast by the OBR.

Higher spending on welfare and pensions due to inflation is also expected to increase borrowing, though it is forecast to fall as a share of the economy over the next five years.

However, forecasts are only a best guess at what might happen in the future. Given the way the conflict in the Middle East has upended previous predictions, the future of the war could alter inflation expectations.

US President Donald Trump has suggested the war will end after the mid-term elections next month.

The OBR admitted there remained "significant uncertainty" around its predictions due to the changing situation in the Middle East.

title: What the Budget offers for under 25s - and what it leaves out
text:
Chancellor John Healey has announced his Budget, which includes changes to minimum wage and help for people trying to get onto the housing ladder.

Here is how the Budget could affect you if you are under-25.

If you are an 18-to-20 year-old earning the minimum wage, your pay will go up by 3.9% from next April.

However, the increase may be lower than you had expected. That is because Healey reversed course on how his Labour predecessor, Rachel Reeves, had been increasing the minimum wage for young people.

Labour had promised to do away with "discriminatory age bands", with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage. This year, 18-20 year-olds will see the same increase as older workers, meaning the disparity will remain. So, for 18-to-20 year-olds, your pay will rise to £11.27, while over-20s will be paid a minimum of £13.21 an hour.

The increase also means a 21-year-old, who is working full time on the minimum wage and took out a student loan after 2023, will now earn enough to meet the £25,000 repayment threshold, over which they will start paying back 9% of their earnings.

The Budget contained plans to help people get onto the housing ladder, including the introduction of a "First Time Buyer Isa". This is an account in which savers can build up a deposit, with the government topping up contributions of up to £4,000 each year with a 25% bonus.

The new savings account will be introduced in 2029, replacing the existing Lifetime Isa, which has been criticised by some for imposing harsh penalties on those buying homes for more than the £450,000 cap.

The cap will remain, but the new "First Time Buyer Isa" will ensure savers are not penalised by losing their own money when making withdrawals. Savers will only lose contributions made by the government when making withdrawals which are not eligible for the account.

The penalty for withdrawals from existing Lifetime Isas will be lowered, too, to address concerns about savers being punished.

The government had already revealed a £4.7bn scheme for first-time buyers in England dubbed Your First Home. It is aiming to help 70,000 individuals and couples get on the housing ladder

The scheme will allow people to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It will provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.

Capped at £110,000 outside London and £140,000 in the capital, it is aimed at those hoping to get on the housing ladder without help from "the bank of mum and dad".

If you are a young person hoping to start a business in England, the Budget contained good news for you.

The chancellor wants to level the playing field for young entrepreneurs who have bright ideas, but who might not have the same family financial backing as others.

In an attempt to encourage more young people to start their own businesses, the government will pilot a "Young Entrepreneurs Allowance" in England.

The allowance will see your living costs partly covered by the government for the first year your business is operating. Healey hopes it will encourage more young people to take the plunge and become entrepreneurs.

Details of the scheme are thin at the moment, however, only that it will be rolled out "shortly".

Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite its range of small measures

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you

If you are one of more than a million 18-to-24 year-olds not in employment, education or training (Neet), Wednesday's Budget may have been a frustrating watch.

The chancellor acknowledged the scale of the crisis facing young people, but said solutions would not come yet. Ministers are waiting on a series of recommendations from Alan Milburn, who has been looking into why so many young people are Neet in the UK.

Milburn has warned Britain is " at risk of a lost generation " due to the crisis, saying a "round of ammunition" is needed rather than a silver bullet. He will make recommendations to the government later this year.

Healey said he refused to write off young people during his Budget speech and the government was looking forward to Milburn's final report.

Another group left hanging were those with outstanding student loans, particularly the controversial Plan 2 loans taken out between 2012 and 2023 - which many fear they will never be able to pay off.

If you have student loans, the government has said it is looking at ways to reform the repayment system. But action was not forthcoming at the Budget, despite expectations in the run up that the issue might be addressed.

After the statement, Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds said the loan repayment system is "under review".

"We inherited a system that is difficult and unfair on young people, but we weren't able to move on that today," she told the BBC.

title: Sesko ruled out until January with shin injury
text:
Manchester United striker Benjamin Sesko is expected to be out until at least January with a shin injury.

The 23-year-old has not featured for the club since their defeat by Brighton in the Carabao Cup on 16 September, when he was substituted in the 66th minute.

The Slovenia international required multiple tests to try to get to the bottom of the problem, with manager Michael Carrick frequently asking when he will be fit to return.

Sources say the issue is not shin splints but an impact injury, which is not quite the same as the initial problem.

Sesko missed all of pre-season with the complaint, which also plagued him last season and flared up against Liverpool in May, causing him to miss the final three Premier League matches.

Since joining United from RB Leipzig in a deal worth £73.7m in August 2025, Sesko has made 38 appearances in all competitions, contributing 14 goals and one assist.

Despite missing eight matches, he was their joint-highest goalscorer (11) in the Premier League last season alongside Bryan Mbeumo.

His absence has been keenly felt as it has robbed Carrick of his only orthodox number nine.

Sesko has scored two goals this term, against Everton in the Premier League and Sabah FK in the Champions League. After that match he spoke about his relief at being injury free. Sadly that did not last.

Sesko will now miss crucial Premier League games, including meetings with Liverpool and Arsenal, and at least three matches in the Champions League.

It remains to be seen if the problem forces United to make a move in the January transfer window as a relative lack of an orthodox forward has been cited as a reason for their chronic recent form.

United are currently languishing in 16th place, with their only league win against Ipswich on 30 August, and are without a win in all competitions since 10 September.

Following last Wednesday's 4-1 loss against Como in the Champions League, captain Bruno Fernandes criticised the tactics of manager Carrick.

The Portugal international was an unused substitute during United's 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth on Sunday, but the pair have reportedly held clear-the-air talks on Tuesday.

Carrick was widely expected to be sacked following the Bournemouth defeat, but will take charge against Chelsea on Saturday (12:30 GMT).

title: Healey provides some breathing space but things still set to get worse for most
text:
John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.

It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses – and the government's ability to help.

While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.

The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes.

Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament. On that basis, it could be the second worse parliament for living standards, after the last one, since the 1950s - a sign of how far the war has blown prosperity off course.

But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.

Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%

However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by £14bn in the past year alone.

The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.

As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be £160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.

And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.

So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.

The markets seem reassured – even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you

So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.

Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas – justice and higher education for example – are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.

There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.

And issues around the other big area of spending – welfare – remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by £100bn.

The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further £13bn.

Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.

Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution – but there is much to be fleshed out.

And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.

Between regulation and higher costs – in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.

So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.

With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.

The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.

So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.

For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.

A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.

title: Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget
text:
Millions of households will get £100 to help with soaring energy bills to be paid for by a tax on bank profits, John Healey has announced in his first Budget.

The chancellor said he wanted to give hard-pressed families "breathing space now" and "hope for the future" as the UK economy is battered by "global economic storms".

He also unveiled tax breaks to boost high street businesses - but confirmed that many big decisions, including on defence spending and welfare, will not be made until next year.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Healey's plans were "not bold enough" and the government was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".

In an hour-long speech to a packed House of Commons, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other frontbench colleagues cheering him on, the chancellor unveiled a string of measures aimed at cutting the cost of living.

One-off £100 energy payment for people living in council tax bands A to D in England, with Wales saying it will match the payment and the Scottish government planning to "replicate" it

Gas standing charges in England, Scotland and Wales, to be scrapped during 2027 "or as soon as possible after". These fixed daily fees will be shifted onto the price of each unit of energy, meaning heavy gas users will face higher bills

Extending the 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel to July

Increasing minimum wage rates by 3.9% in April, although there will be no progress on narrowing the gap between rates for older and younger workers

Healey increased the tax on the profits of big banks from 3% to 6%, which will last from January next year to April 2028, and increased taxes on high-stakes gambling machines.

Healey announces £100 energy bill help for millions and raises taxes on banks and some savers

Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you

Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite its range of small measures

As part of a package to help business, Healey increased the point at which High Street shops in England start paying business rates from £12,000 to £18,000, with vape shops and adult gaming centres excluded from the relief.

But he had little scope for big giveaways as the public finances remain stretched, with the UK set to spend £14bn more on debt interest payments this year.

Income tax thresholds will remain frozen and the tax on income from savings and property rental will rise to 24% for basic rate taxpayers from April 2027, after it had been scheduled to go up to 22%.

But a cut to the cash ISA allowance from £20,000 a year to £12,000, announced last year by Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves, will be axed.

The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) downgraded its growth forecast for next year to 1%, with slightly higher increases predicted for subsequent years.

In its latest assessment, the OBR said British households were set to be little better off than before the Covid pandemic even a decade after Covid-19 hit, a situation the watchdog's boss David Miles described as "pretty grim".

In his Budget speech, Healey repeatedly stressed that the UK economy was being battered by "global uncertainties" and soaring oil prices caused by conflict in the Middle East.

"Those are the storms we face. We can't wish them away. We must choose the course we steer through them," he told MPs.

Healey also used his speech to announce plans to allow regional mayors to keep 20% of business rates and a share of income tax to spend on local priorities.

The aim was to allow mayors to retain 100% of business rates raised in their areas by the end of the decade, he added, in "the most radical act of devolution in a generation".

And he sought to address opposition claims the Labour government is unwilling to cut benefits, insisting that both he and Burnham were committed to bringing down the welfare bill in a "Labour way".

But he said no decisions would be taken until reviews by Alan Milburn , into young people not in work or training, and Stephen Timms, on Personal Independence Payments , had been published, with legislation to follow next year.

The £4.7bn black hole in the defence investment plan will be funded, the chancellor revealed, in part through taking money from capital budgets across Whitehall.

Healey said he will set out how the government plans to meet its commitment to spend 3% of the national income on defence by 2030, and 3.5% by 2035, at next year's spending review.

But Badenoch said he "should have set out a plan for 3% today," highlighting his claim when he resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June that UK forces were at risk due to a lack of cash.

"So now he is the man who is increasing risk to personnel on operations, he is the man who is making our country less safe, he has failed his own test," the Conservative leader said.

"This is on him and no-one will ever forget. If he had any decency he would resign again today."

The Tory leader said that with the UK heading for a record tax burden and "spending more on debt interest than on the army and schools combined", Healey's Budget was "not good enough, not strong enough, not bold enough".

Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the Budget "has a raft of fiddly measures but very little that will move the dial on growth".

Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said that until the government has "the courage" to fix the UK's trading relationship with the EU any Budget will just be "tinkering around the edges" and will not provide the growth the country needs.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the Budget was full of "little giveaways" but "doesn't overall do very much" and did not offer "anything of any value on defence whatsoever".

Healey also faced criticism from the left, with the general secretary of the Unite union, Sharon Graham describing the cost of living measures in the Budget as "baby steps".…

title: 'I can still win this day' - Alison Jackson recovers from mechanical to win middle stage at seven-day Gravel Burn
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
Alison Jackson (St Michel-Preference Home-Auber93) ignited the fourth day of racing at Nedbank Gravel Burn as the elite women contested their first bunch sprint, and the Canadian scored the unexpected victory after recovering from a mechanical.

Jackson returned for her second appearance at the weeklong 750km South African gravel stage race, where she finished 11th overall last year, and was looking for her first stage win.

“I approached this year differently; last year I had a surf camp ahead of the event but this year I kept riding, so I had no excuses. The first few days didn’t go to plan with crashes and mechanicals, but you never give up," Jackson told organisers.

Jackson began the opening day of racing from Graaff-Reinet in the lead pack, which was split with 49km to go on the climb of Conical Peak, where Nele Laing (Canyon DT Swiss ATR) accelerated away. Jackson suffered a crash and then struggled in the chase on the hilly 90km route, finishing 7:30 off the pace to begin the week in seventh overall.

The next two stages combined for 242km and nearly 2,000 metres of elevation gain as the race moved south into the Great Karoo, a vast desert-like landscape that translates to 'land of thirst'. The GC standings settled into place with Laing in the lead, South African gravel champion Hayley Preen (ChemChamp Honeycomb) in second place and Clara Koppenburg (Tudor Pro) in third, with Jackson into eighth.

During the loop route Wednesday through valley roads and then a climb back to Merino, Jackson dropped out of the lead group to deal with a battery mechanical on the rear derailleur. As the race camera caught her working on the bike at an aid station, she said, "I can still win this day", and this proved to be a true statement.

She worked her way back on the loose gravel and dry dirt to catch the lead pack, and then surged from the 12-rider group in the closing 500 metres to win the stage.

"I know I can sprint – a sprinter can always sprint at the end; it doesn’t matter how tired you are,” the former Paris-Roubaix champion confirmed after the win. She's had a number of top 10s on the road this year, including stage 4 of the Giro d'Italia plus the time trial and road race at Canadian Nationals. At the UCI Gravel World Series event, The Gralloch, earlier this year, she finished sixth.

Laing comes to the race for the first time fresh off fourth place at UCI Gravel World Championships . She finished safely in the bunch behind Canyon DT Swiss ATR teammates, third place going to Larissa Hartog, who was also third at UCI Gravel Worlds for the Netherlands, and Carolin Schiff in sixth, and Jade Treffeisen going 10th. The German took the first orange leader's jersey with the opening stage win and now has 56 seconds on Preen and 4:14 on Koppenburg.

The men's division saw their second sprint finish of the week so far, stage 4 with 13 riders going to the line in a cloud of dust, with South Africans Travis Stedman (Toyota Specialized Imbuko) and Ryan Gibbons (RoadCover SunGod) going one-two and USA's Cole Davis (SpeedStudio) in third.

GC leader Matthew Beers (Toyota Specialized) let the breakaway go and finished 2:41 back, marking his rivals, with second-placed Filippo Colombo (Scott-SRAM) 32 seconds back and third-placed Tristan Nortje (Toyota Specialized Imbuko) at 51 seconds.

The final three stages take the riders to Gwanishi and the southernmost point at the Shamwari Private Game Reserve in the south. Beers seeks a second consecutive GC title, while defending women's champion Axelle Dubau-Prevot (EF Education-Oatly) has work to do to move from 13th position and 8:23 from Laing.

title: Howe, Nagelsmann, Pochettino: can anyone end Manchester United’s doom loop?
author: Daniel Harris
text:
Even an elite coach would surely struggle at Old Trafford amid the executive chaos and with an unfit, uneven squad

I n January 2014 the 13th series of Celebrity Big Brother aired in the UK, the show so popular that its run time was extended by five days before a public vote anointed Jim Davidson the winner. Then, two years later when Brexit happened, people wondered where their tolerant country had gone, lamenting the ephemeral spirit of London 2012 as though the 2011 riots were some kind of fever dream, not a desperate response to decades of structural and institutional racism exacerbated by the cruelty of unnecessary austerity.

The truth is that if security is quickly upended, it was built on quicksand to begin with. Which brings us to Manchester United, easing effortlessly from an uplifting third-place finish to some of the worst football in their history.

It is entirely possible that Alex Ferguson made a deal with the devil to the effect that United would be great until he retired and hilariously dreadful thereafter. But assuming not, his l’état, c’est moi mentality was busy setting up the post-him fall even at the height of the success – itself a consequence of what had gone before.

A day after the Munich air disaster, Louis Edwards – later a seller of condemned meat to schools – joined the board, eventually assuming control thanks to a dodgy rights issue. He bequeathed the club to Martin – his substellar son – who floated it for personal gain, turning an institution that sought to win, entertain and unify into a business legally compelled to return value to shareholders.

This left United vulnerable to acquisition by anyone and, when Ferguson fell out with two directors – a horse, a horse, his kingdom for a horse’s ejaculate – they sold to the Glazers, who loaded the purchase price and accordant interest obligation on to the club, with government and football authorities waving through a move since outlawed. Ferguson, meanwhile, must have feared exactly what the takeover would entail and known that without his support the banks might not have lent the money, while the chief executive David Gill admitted opposition to it but stayed in his role anyway, and so the pillaging began.

The English game then exploded, with investment in United left available only to those of wealth so extreme it necessarily casts aspersions over their character – such as arch polluter and anti‑immigration zealot, Jim Ratcliffe. Proclaiming inaccurate and divisive rhetoric contrary to the inclusive, cosmopolitan spirit of Manchester and United, jobs were culled and fights picked with fans, Old Trafford’s most desirable seats socially cleansed so the club could sell them to day-trippers for astronomical prices, with longstanding supporters banned after trumped-up charges of touting – a deeply principled stance the club fails to apply to itself.

Not untypically for a billionaire, Ratcliffe seemingly believes that correct opinions reflect exchequer not expertise, giving himself final say on footballing decisions. And rather than the “best in class” executives he promised, his United operate according to what political analysts call the “Boris principle”, no‑marks in thrall to their own self‑image given jobs for which they lack the ability and character, the consequent chaos being effective sabotage.

So the patterns continue: Champions League qualification is missed, insufficient funds are released; a new unsuitable manager spends heavily on players below requisite standard; Champions League qualification is achieved via unsustainably reactive style; the manager is denied necessary funds amounting to less than the bounty of Champions League qualification; the manager imposes a proactive style without the necessary materials; the manager is belatedly fired for a fee far exceeding that saved by cutting jobs; a new unsuitable manager, with entirely different requirements to his predecessor, is appointed; executive accountability is absent.

It is thus no surprise that Michael Carrick remains unfired , despite exuding the vibe of a man who’s mentally fired himself. Perhaps it’s a stay of execution, but more likely there’s bizarre hope of a turnaround, partly to save paying him off, partly because the relevant executives can’t achieve consensus on a replacement, and partly because surely even Omar Berrada and Jason Wilcox accept that, following another catastrophe, after dismissing Carrick they are honour-bound to dismiss themselves.

Except they and United don’t work like that.

So, just as they failed Carrick by not recruiting properly ; failing to add experience to his coaching team; failing to replace outgoing fitness and set-piece coaches and failing to interrogate details of his new game-model, they are now failing him by having him continue in a job that is too much for him, destroying a season that remains salvageable. Meantime, the Glazers’ dividends continue unabated.

As such, the question isn’t so much who should be United’s next manager as can anyone manage United? Increasingly, it looks like the answer is – to quote Don Logan in Sexy Beast – “No”.

There are immediate on‑pitch issues: the team are unfit and their collective mentality weak; after years being lied to, the captain has finally broken; and the players hate the suits, the package toxic. Those are the minor problems.

Roughly, football management comprises five aspects: coaching, tactics, talent ID, pastoral care and presence. And, though no manager excels in every department, at this version of United surely they must. Moreover, given this is no job for a novice, track record is also important – and it might be here that Unai Emery’s candidature falls down, his brilliance in transforming mid‑ranking clubs undermined by failures at two high-profile basket cases.…

title: 'He's now one of the big stars in cycling' – Can Visma fit British rider Matthew Brennan into Tour de France plans alongside Vingegaard and Van Aert?
author: James Moultrie
text:
With the Tour de France Grand Départ taking place in Great Britain in 2027, and a likely sprint into the Carlisle stage offering up the first yellow jersey, Matthew Brennan (Visma-Lease a Bike) represents the best chance at an opening day home winner. But will the rising British star even be present?

Riding for the same team as Jonas Vingegaard and Wout van Aert means that any kind of stage-hunting opportunities are going to be limited, but Brennan has shown throughout 2026 that he can be relied upon for victories, and as a perfect accompaniment to the Belgian star's talents.

Throughout the Vuelta a España, Brennan and Van Aert combined perfectly as Visma dominated the flat and punchy days, winning a third of the 21 stages – five for the Brit and two for the Belgian – across sprints and breakaways.

"It's my first Grand Tour, but also to be as successful in this first Grand Tour is a really nice step into the ambition to try and win in the first few stages in the Tour de France next year," said Brennan.

"I've seen the first and also the second stage [of the 2027 Tour, and the third is quite hard, but there are definitely opportunities to do something within my strengths.

"I would really like to be on the start line. I also understand that the best squad has to go with the ambitions the team has, but I think that for the moment, with being successful as a team, we can probably use myself in different ways to help Jonas bring out his strengths even more and play the cards.

"But that's also just something the team will discuss in the future, and there has been no decision made, so we just take it as it comes and go from there."

With the full route confirmed in Paris earlier this month, it confirmed more than just two or three chances for Brennan on home roads, but a Tour filled with flat days and punchy finales, where he can potentially challenge the top sprinters and the likes of Mathieu van der Poel and Tadej Pogačar .

Visma are considering Brennan, and team boss Richard Plugge couldn't deny that the Brit was going to make up a big part of their plans in 2027, having taken the same number of pro wins as Vingegaard this past season: 12.

"He's entered a small group of very big riders, I think. And when he came to the team, we already knew when he started sprint training, etc. We thought, 'Whoa, what is happening here?' And you see how he climbs here with the best punchy climbers on a parcours like this, then it's really promising for the future," Plugge told at the finish of the last stage in Granada.

"But it's also his first Grand Tour, and I told him just now to just be really proud: five stage wins – that's incredible, but also finishing your first Grand Tour will only make you stronger and your motor bigger.

"Let's wait and see for the Tour… Let us evaluate and make plans for next year. Obviously, he's part of our plans also with Wout and with Jonas [for 2027], so we will discuss with the whole team like we always do in the coming weeks, and then in our training camp, when we have a media day, we will tell you."

Visma's media day will arrive on December 17, when the full schedules for their big leaders will be revealed, alongside provisional squads for the Tour, which Brennan will desperately hope he's on.

Plugge and all of the management at Visma will have the main goal of winning back the yellow jersey from Pogačar, as they did in 2022 and 2023, but there is little harm in including one stage hunter in Brennan to the ranks.

He's already shown his versatility as a winner and helper for Van Aert, so he would be more than willing and capable to support Vingegaard on the punchier days where victory isn't potentially on the cards. Plugge has some deciding to do, but Brennan signing his future with Visma until 2029 suggests he's confident he'll get the opportunities he wants, even with the Dutch squad's other priorities.

"Matthew knocked very hard on the door there," he told , referring to the Brit's five stage wins from the Vuelta. "You know that he is now one of the big stars in cycling. And this is the biggest race. So we are certainly going to consider it."

title: 'It feels like coming full circle' – Australian DS Matt White rejoins EF Education-EasyPost 16 years after departing
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
White, who hung up his wheels as a racer in 2007, began his directing career at the team, staying there for three years before being dismissed over a breach of policy. He then completed a long stint at Jayco-AlUla.

"It feels like coming full circle. I started my career as a sports director here back in 2008," said White.

"I've obviously spent a lot of time away, but it's a team that I've always kept very close to my heart. It's exciting to come back to a team that has so many talented young riders and a lot of ambition to develop this group over a long period of time."

White, who will join an EF DS team that includes Charly Wegelius, Ken Vanmarcke and Tom Southam, said he's excited by the team's attacking ethos and added that he's looking forward to working with the young riders at the team.

"I think the beauty of going for stages is that it's all or nothing. You're all in for the day, then you might have a day or two when you're not, and then you're all in again. Especially in a Grand Tour, I think that's a really exciting mindset and way to approach a race," he said.

"The most exciting thing about this group is that it's such a young, talented team. You just don't know what these athletes are capable of on any given day.

"Nurturing those guys and getting the best out of them, both as individuals and as a group, is an exciting challenge for me. Working with riders who don't yet know where their ceiling is, and helping them discover what they're capable of, is something that gets me up in the morning."

Ben Healy and Neilson Powless will lead the team next season, while Iván Sosa, Tao Geoghegan Hart, and Lorenzo Milesi are among six confirmed additions.

White said that success for him and EF next year will be measured by featuring throughout the season and getting results at the biggest races of the calendar.

"My passion is getting the most out of people. Cycling has changed a lot, but there's one thing that hasn't changed: you're dealing with human beings," he said.

"Getting the most out of people is something I really enjoy. I think if, in 12 months' time, we can sit back and look at the season and see that we've featured prominently throughout the year, especially at the pointy end of the races that matter, then that's a measure of success. And those races are the three Grand Tours and a lot of the Monuments."

White rode as a professional between 1996 and 2007 before joining what is now EF, and was then Garmin-Chipotle, for his first directing role in 2008. That stint with the team lasted only three seasons, before he was dismissed for breaching team policies by referring a rider to an outside doctor without reference to the team's own medical staff.

title: Perez signs multi-year extension with Cadillac
text:
Sergio Perez will remain with Cadillac until 2029 after signing a multi-year contract extension.

The 36-year-old, who is set to celebrate his 300th Grand Prix start in his home race in Mexico City this weekend, joined the American Formula One team last August before their debut season on the grid, racing alongside fellow veteran Valtteri Bottas.

Perez made his Formula One debut in 2011 and has won six grands prix – five for Red Bull between 2021-24 and one for Racing Point (now Aston Martin) in 2020.

He finished third in the 2022 drivers' championship and second behind team-mate Max Verstappen in 2023.

Despite having two years left on his contract, he was dropped by Red Bull at the end of the 2024 season after the team felt he had run out of time to prove he could support Verstappen.

Perez sits bottom of the 2026 standings, with three 14th-place finishes – in Barcelona, Silverstone, and Azerbaijan – his best performances. Neither he nor Bottas has earned a point for Cadillac.

"Joining Cadillac from day one was a project I truly believed in, and extending my commitment feels like a natural continuation of this chapter," said Perez.

"Building a Formula One team from the ground up takes time, relentless work and patience, but the progress we are making together is incredibly rewarding.

"There is still a lot of work ahead of us and I am fully committed to the next three years."

title: The Factor Sarana Proves Weight Isn’t Everything in Gravel
author: Josh Ross
text:
Optional front suspension 57mm tire clearance Frame storage leaf-spring seat-stay system 52-tooth max chainring Available as a chassis only

The idea of the 2027 Velo Field Test is to look at today’s gravel bikes and try to identify the direction things are going, to figure out what the future of gravel looks like. Our choice for this is the Factor Sarana, and I personally could not be happier.

The Factor Sarana is designed to be an ultra-endurance race bike. It’s a category of bike that some people say isn’t real, yet it was the winning bike for this year’s Tour Divide race. It was also, realistically speaking, a bike designed with Factor athlete Rob Britton in mind. That seems like a real category of racing to me, and it’s also a category that actually applies very well to many other types of racing and everyday riders. Perhaps call it endurance gravel if that makes more sense to you.

The bike you’d want for ultra-endurance racing is, in many ways, an all-around bike. It’s not so aggressive that you can’t hold the position for days of racing. It’s a bike that helps you when you can barely think straight, and it won’t punish you if you get distracted. A good ultra-endurance bike is also a bike that keeps you comfortable over long distances.

If you are thinking that maybe a bike with those qualities sounds pretty good for you, you aren’t alone. Comfortable, predictable, and capable are perfect traits for most people riding bikes, and that’s why we felt like the Sarana was a good candidate for the future direction of gravel riding. I happen to be thrilled because ultra-endurance is my passion, so if that’s the direction we are going, great. Let’s talk about what I like, and what I don’t, about the Factor Sarana.

I have to admit that one of the things I love about the Sarana is that it’s targeting a part of the market that I really enjoy. Never mind that this is a gravel bike for a moment; think in terms of road bikes. Inherently, this is an endurance bike, and endurance bikes tend to lack appeal. People are not drawn to the sensible bike, so on the road side, it becomes an “all-road” bike—despite really not being that in many cases. What does a brand do on the gravel side? You can’t sprinkle in some gravel marketing; it’s already a gravel bike. The solution seems to have been to focus on ultra-endurance as a way to jazz this up.

That’s the most cynical way to view it, though. Instead, think about what ultra-endurance actually demands and how that translates to a bike. It also happens to align with Factor athletes, and that makes it authentic.

To bring this to a point: what I like about the Factor Sarana is the leaf-spring rear triangle design. What I’m talking about is a system that we’ve seen other brands take various passes at, but Factor is a company that takes pride in carbon engineering. Rather than employ a mechanical hinge like Cannondale, Factor started by dropping the chainstays near the bottom bracket. This design allows for the necessary space of 57mm tire clearance with a 425mm chainstay, but it also creates a curve that arcs gracefully up before finally curving down at the rear axle. Then, right at the top of that apex, where the design puts the most leverage on the chainstay, it’s intentionally flattened and thinned.

This chainstay design is also paired with a curved seat tube that has deeply dropped seatstays. That provides a designated flex point in the seat tube, with the seatstay positioned exactly where it needs to be to push on it and drive that movement.

This shaping results in a lot of movement in the rear triangle, but it requires nothing from the end user. By utilizing geometry and carbon layup, Factor created a frame that flexes vertically to absorb impacts while remaining laterally stiff for power transfer. You get a bit of suspension without needing to deal with the weight and maintenance of a mechanical system. Factor claims this provides an “18% reduction in vibration amplitude,” and Factor has also thrown a figure of 10mm of travel at me. Either way, the exact math doesn’t matter because the result is that you can feel it, and it’s just there without drawbacks.

This also plays perfectly with the 57mm of tire clearance. Bigger tires mean more suspension and more capability. Combine that with the vertical movement of the rear triangle, and you have this great combination of comfort and capability without dealing with the bobbing or maintenance of a shock system.

Weight. This bike is heavy. We tested the suspension version, and ready to ride (minus pedals), it came in at 9.58 kg (21.1 lbs). Of course, a large part of what some of the team appreciated while testing in Squamish was that front suspension. My personal take is that while the RockShox fork felt great when out of the saddle, I’d prefer the bike without it. Unfortunately, ditching the fork doesn’t fully solve the issue.

Even if you take that suspension away, it’s still a ~1,200g frame. In fact, we can do a bit of math: the rigid fork is 550 grams according to Factor, and the suspension fork is roughly 1,260 grams. In theory, swapping those out leaves you with an 8.87 kg (19.55 lb) bike built with SRAM Force—and saddled with a premium price tag.

To put that in perspective, the version we tested came in heavier than the 32-inch, metal-framed Salsa Fargo, and nearly matches the Pivot Les SL drop-bar mountain bike. Of course, our Field Test was designed to include wildly different bikes, so if we instead look at the Cannondale Topstone Carbon 1 AXS Lefty as a more direct comparison, the Sarana is slightly lighter at 9.58 kg versus 9.8 kg. However, the Cannondale is also $2,000 less and comes with SRAM Rival instead of Force.…

title: Netcompany Ineos to use AI-based aero testing app from 2027
author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)
text:
Netcompany Ineos are set to reveal a partnership with digital aerodynamics app, AiRO, which will see it use a consumer-available app and artificial intelligence for its aero testing in the 2027 season.

The AiRO app, which launched a new AI-based CFD simulation tool called Vayu on Wednesday, promises to bring aero testing to a broader audience via bike fitters across the world.

It was founded just 14 months ago, and already claims to have multiple other WorldTour teams as paying customers.

AiRO confirmed it will be working with Netcompany Ineos in 2027, and understands a fuller announcement of the partnership will be made next week.

Founder, Ingmar Jungnickel – who cut his teeth with the German Olympic team, Specialized’s S-Racing division and the development of the last edition Specialized S-Works Venge – founded the company as a spin-off from a similar project he developed for the USA speedskating squad.

He ran a select group of media, including through the AiRO app, which spans road, gravel, mountain bike, and time trialling.

The app is available to anyone via specialist bike fitters for approximately $200 per session, and works by creating a 'digital twin' of each rider.

Using photographs, specialised software turns the images into a 3D simulation of the rider, which you can use to then run app-based aero experiments, such as swapping helmets or adjusting the rider’s position.

By integrating AI and its new 'Vayu' add-on, Jungnickel explains he has generated a long list of potential benefits.

One of these, which he caveats is a future innovation currently under construction, is the ability to instantly test 20+ different helmets (which have already been scanned into the app) on one rider, each in dozens of head positions, effectively recreating over 400 wind tunnel tests at the click of a button.

If Josh Tarling stops wearing a Kask helmet next year, we may able to attribute that decision to this feature, but there are of course other sponsorship agreements to navigate there.

A second feature is to immediately test over 100 small rider position changes – arms, head, shrug, etc – and order them by the available improvement. Working with the bike fitter, the rider can then replicate these positions to check whether they are actually achievable and sustainable in the real world.

The Netcompany Ineos deal is the brand’s first official partnership with a team, but based on existing work with teams, Jungnickel’s expectation is that the British squad will use it alongside real wind tunnel testing to help with testing the full squad rather than just the top riders, without the increased time and financial commitment that doing so in a wind tunnel would need.

He also says teams are excited by the opportunity to test riders' road bike positions, which he says takes longer and is less repeatable in a wind tunnel or velodrome setting.

Finally, he predicts that by having a digital twin of all the team's riders, the team will be able to quickly and cheaply test ideas, without needing the rider present.

And from there, if a new, faster position is found, but where a biomechanical concern exists, they can work with coaches and biomechanics experts to formulate a plan before the rider makes the switch and potentially causes an injury.

The full scope of the partnership is still being worked out, and details are expected to follow soon.

title: Sometimes Halloween Candy is Better than Energy Gels for Your Workout. Here’s Why.
author: Jim Cotton
text:
Cyclists who are sick of the frightening cost and ghastly gloop of energy gels should consider dressing as a demon and going trick-or-treating this Halloween.

The candy that will be dished out to expectant ghouls and gremlins this weekend is almost perfect riding fuel.

Kids’ favorites like Nerds Gummy Clusters, Sour Patch Kids, and the ever-controversial candy corn can deliver 10 times more energy per dollar and multiple times more flavor per mouthful than primo sports nutrition products.

But before you go craft a costume and muster a trick-or-treat patrol, there are a few things you should know.

They might save your candy-fueled bike rides from becoming a fright.

Carbs are the body’s preferred source of fast energy , but they’re a limited resource. The muscles and liver can only store a limited amount of carbohydrates, making it essential to top up during any longer, harder ride. Those who don’t face the prospect of an empty fuel tank and a miserable slog home.

Halloween candy provides exactly what the working muscles need: fast-acting, low-fiber carbohydrates.

At the basic level, it’s no different from the gels and drinks that promise to bonk-proof your ride with perfectly synthesized packages of energy.

And we all know the promise of sport nutrition comes at a price. A packet of “pina colada” or “birthday cake” flavor sports goo can cost close to five bucks.

When we compared the cost and nutritional values of nine popular Halloween candies to some of our favored gels, the results were not surprising.

A couple of handfuls of candy will deliver the same amount of carbohydrate as a leading energy gel, at just a fraction of the price.

For example, per our calculations, every gram of carbohydrate in a hyper-researched Maurten hydrogel costs 11 cents. One gram of carbohydrate from the Halloween love-or-hate candy corn costs one cent.

So that’s it, right? No energy gels, ever again?

Not all carbs are created equal, and candy carbs are not always the best carbs for workout fuel – no matter how damn cheap and tasty they might be.

The modern sports nutrition that enabled the high-carb fueling “revolution ” uses specific sugar blends to maximize carbohydrate absorption into the gut and oxidation by the muscles.

By using both glucose and fructose in 1:0.8 or 2:1 ratios, leading products allow athletes like Tadej Pogačar to fuel at more than 500 calories of carbs per hour, for six hours straight.

Try that with a bag of Twizzlers; we dare you. Maybe stash some toilet paper in your jersey pocket if you do.

Mass-market candy rarely, if ever, uses the glucose-to-fructose ratios that have saved the WorldTour from the explosive G.I. distress that once haunted high-carb fueling. Targeting the pro-standard 120 grams of carbs per hour with a packet of Sour Patch Kids will result in scenes worthy of the most icky horror movie.

If you hope to “train hard” rather than just “ride,” skip the sweeties. Invest in your workout and splurge on sports nutrition.

In many cases, energy gels and drinks are not just energy.

Many products are boosted with stimulants like caffeine or taurine, or minerals like sodium and potassium.

Electrolyte supplementation can be especially important for any rider going long or going hard. Candy won’t help keep sodium balance in check.

By contrast, candies can include things you might not want in the fueling mix.

Fiber and fats are not your friends if you need fast energy. They slow digestion, and can cause gut rot if eaten during workout intensity.

So, we’re sorry to say it, Snickers fans. That delicious stick of chocolate and nuts might wreck your workout. Save it for when you get home – your stomach will thank you, and your jersey lining might, too. There’s no coming back from finding a melted chocolate bar smooshed into your back pocket after a long or hot ride.

If you want fast fuel, choose your Halloween candy carefully. Nerds Gummy Clusters, Sour Patch Kids, and Skittles will give you more speed than Snickers or Reese’s.

But that’s not to say chocolate doesn’t have a place in your cycling cupboard.

For long, low-intensity rides, chocolate’s satiety and slower-release energy can see you right for endless kilometers. Just ask Oreo and Payday bar afficionado , Lachlan Morton.

But for the sake of your sleek new apparel, consider how you carry it.

And perhaps two of the most obvious considerations when considering gels vs. candy: Portability and munch-ability.

As tasty as Nerds Gummy Clusters might be, anyone who’s tried chewing them down mid-effort is in for a fright. The choking hazard of small candies is very real if you’re trying to hit a workout.

And that’s if you can even access them while on the move.

An easily overlooked benefit of an energy gel is just how easy it is to access and open while you’re clinging to the wheels of the weekend group ride. Ever tried tearing open a packet of Sour Patch Kids with frozen mid-winter fingers while riding 350 watts? Trust us, don’t bother.

A couple of real-food fueling transportation tips?

Pre-open candy packets before you go ride for easy accessibility.

And if you can’t face a six-hour ride without a Twix, we get it. But stash it in the bar bag, not the pocket of your $150 jersey.

Considering some over-age trick-or-treating this weekend?

Here’s how Team Velo ’s favorite candies compare to some leading energy gels to help guide your Halloween ghouling.

We’ve included the costs and total nutritional values of packet sizes often found in a local store, and added our golden metric: cost per carbohydrate.

We’ve also included some reasonable serving sizes for cyclists meticulous enough to split an XL sack of sweets into portions before they ride.

Candy can give you 10 times more carbs per dollar than sport nutrition.

Candy corn worked out as the cheapest of all the grocery store treats, but could you handle the polarizing, waxy consistency?…

title: 'He has a very long way to go' - 19-year-old Tofik Beshir continues recovery in hospital from horrific training crash as CXD Trek Bikes teammates offer support with 'endless supply of bracelets'
author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
text:
It has been 20 days since Tofik Beshir went on a gravel ride near his college in North Carolina and was air-flighted to a nearby trauma hospital after being struck head-on by a driver of a motor vehicle. He was allowed to relocate to a Washington, D.C.-area hospital to be near his family, but "there's a long road ahead" according to his cyclo-cross team manager at CXD Trek Bikes.

"I can say he is much more conscious than he has been the prior week. Having Tofik talk back, even with his raspy voice, is just wonderful. I'm looking forward to when he can say thank you to the world," Chris Merriam, founder and team manager for CXD Trek Bikes, told .

Beshir first received medical care at Johnson City Medical Center in east Tennessee, with "injuries consistent with brain shear trauma". Before his parents could travel from Virginia to be at the ICU, Lees-McRae College cycling team coach Timothy Hall and school President Dr. [Herbert l.] Lee King were at Beshir's bedside. He also had Kelly Benefits road team coach and mentor Mark Frazier present. Hall has provided some updates on Instagram, with Beshir's family asking for privacy.

"He was just on a pretty short recovery ride in North Carolina. Both his [Lees-McRae] coach and I were expecting calls from him that night," Merriam recalled. "One of his teammates was actually able to ride to where the sirens were [heard that day] and kind of put everything in motion. Lees McRae and their support system jumped into action, and then we learned about it."

Merriam, who is based in Washington, D.C., said the young riders on his team have been deeply disturbed by the situation. Beshir started with the team as a junior several years ago and opened this season with five wins in six races, sweeping elite races at Charm City Cross en route to winning the USCX Series title and establishing himself as a leader.

Beshir was back in North Carolina for school in early October and preparing for race weekends in Ohio and Indiana, where last year he landed his first UCI elite men's cyclo-cross podiums, including a first UCI elite race victory, at the age of 18, at Major Taylor Cross Cup.

When the news of Beshir's horrific crash was relayed to riders on October 9, Merriam said his CXD teammates wondered if travel and racing in Ohio was "the right thing to do".

"It's a really hard thing to balance going out and racing, just doing the sport, and knowing that our teammate and close friend is lying in a hospital bed. The response from the team [has been huge]. Alyssa [Sarkisov] and Miles [Mattern] in particular, they really led the charge."

He described how team members gathered supplies to hand thread beads onto elastic bands, many in the purple and gold colours for the CXD squad, the day before the race in Ohio. On the first day, he said more than half the field of elites wore the 'Tofik bracelets', including rivals and elite winners Manon Bakker and Andrew Strohmeyer.

"It was thanks to them and Cora Cusack, one of our junior riders, who just made boxes full of them. We were also able to get cards, about 100, so people could send Tofik a note. My wife and I took the cards to him last night, and more from another local race. His mom is helping him work his way through this giant pile of cards.

"I know from him it really means quite a bit the amount of community support he's getting. Whatever people want to call it, prayers or positive healing vibes, he is definitely aware.

"A shout out to Finnley Sonnemann, another one of our juniors. He went to a farmer's market and sold a few hundred dollars of them, which went straight to the GoFundMe."

The GoFundMe page was started on October 9 and has raised $142,157 to date. Merriam said to get the word out right away at Kings CX, the team also created a poster with a QR code, and they hoped to spearhead the crowdsourcing effort into a medical trust for care over time.

"The poster was there when people were coming to pick the bracelets and fill out the cards. It was everybody making donations at whatever level they felt comfortable with, but it made a huge difference. That kind of momentum has really carried forward. It was strange doing what we love, racing, as a team and a family without him."

Trek CXD Bikes will co-host the Pan-American Cyclo-cross Championships in Washington, D.C. on November 7 with the DCMTB club team, the event returning to the Armed Forces Retirement Home. Merriam said a special poster will be created by Marian University cycling alumnus Lucas Stierwalt using a photograph of Beshir popping a wheelie to win a bike race. The posters, as well as "an endless supply of bracelets", will be available at the team tent to continue fundraising efforts.

Merriam confirmed he knew Beshir was healing, though slowly, when the teenager still had his sense of humor.

"I told him that Manon Bakker was racing in Europe with his bracelet, she sent me a message overnight. He said 'I finally get to race in Europe'. So he is internalising all the good feelings."

In addition to the medical trust , his family and collection of teams as that get well cards be sent via US Mail: Tofik Beshir, PO Box 6323, 5636 Connecticut Ave NW, Washington, DC 20015.

title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
author: Peter Beaumont
text:
Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website

Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.

Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.

According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.

Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.

Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi , since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.

Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

title: From scandals and scepticism to parasocial belief – I've witnessed cycling's perception of doping shift dramatically over the last decade, but is that OK?
author: Andy McGrath
text:
"It was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair, we had everything before us, we had nothing before us." - A Tale of Two Cities

The problem was that his emphatic performance coincided with an all-time low in trust in pro cycling; scandal after scandal, lie after lie, burned its followers.

The next morning, a hundred members of the media crammed into a conference room at the Park Inn Hotel in Orange to bury the yellow jersey with demanding questions, not to praise him.

The bombardment began: "What plan do you have to answer the critics suggesting doping may be behind his performance?"

"Yesterday you said you were 'honoured' by the comparison with Lance Armstrong. How can you be honoured given he got all his titles with doping?"

Sat next to him, Team Sky principal Dave Brailsford was also in the crosshairs.

"Dave, can you provide me with your most compelling reason why we should believe not just Chris but every single member of your team?"

The kicker at the end to the race leader: "Is all this beginning to tarnish the whole experience for you?"

"I just think it’s quite sad that we're sitting here the day after the biggest victory of my life, quite a historic win, talking about doping," Froome said. "Quite frankly, my teammates and I have slept on volcanoes to get ready for this, been away for months working our arses off to get here. And here I am basically being accused of being a cheat and a liar. And that's not cool."

With that, the mild-mannered Briton got up and strode out of the room. That spicy 15-minute press conference was a memorable indictment of the crippling lack of belief in the sport.

There was the same cycle after every scandal: talk of rebirth, springs of hope leading to more controversy and winters of despair. Being a cycling fan, let alone a journalist, who believed wholeheartedly in what they were seeing play out on the road was like outing yourself as someone who also thought the Tooth Fairy, Father Christmas and flying pigs existed.

Back then, the sport seemed irredeemably rotten. Every record-breaking ascent raised eyebrows; many superhuman performances were treated as guilty until proven clean, with the baseline assumption that most racers were on something. Doping talk – pharmaceutical and mechanical – was a constant background thrum, asked about in every long-form interview. And if I had a pound for every time I heard or read the going-through-the-motions answer from a bike racer: "the sport is much cleaner now..."

At the pinnacle of performance, Team Sky , Froome and company preached pristine values and zero tolerance to a crowd of angry non-believers. No wonder it occasionally got ugly.

At times, the racing was like a sideshow to the volatile atmosphere between the peloton, spectators and media. Riders felt the frustration and distrust, sometimes physically: Froome had urine thrown at him , was slapped and spat at, super-domestique Richie Porte was punched, and the Sky team car was battered and rocked by spectators on Alpe d'Huez.

The sport is moving from being mired in doubt and traumatised scepticism to a more protective level of fandom – and one of the reasons for that has little to do with pro cycling.

Not so long ago, a rider's primary means of self-expression was limited to interviews with online cycling media or magazines, perhaps a brief appearance on . A comparatively limited output, a slow-burn way of getting to know them.

The digital media landscape has transformed. Social media and video-sharing platforms allow an infinite scroll of unfettered, unfiltered-appearing access, leading to a closer, more parasocial relationship with the sport’s protagonists.

Consequently, traditional print media is no longer the primary storyteller; control of the message has shifted to top riders, squads and brands. Short-form video is king, whether that’s from racers like Victor Campenaerts vlogging authentically pre-race on Instagram or sizable in-house media teams posting curated content for YouTube and other platforms.

With all the proximity over the months and years, a passive, subconscious background swell of positive feeling washes over some followers, driven by personality and good vibes. Doping never comes up organically in their narratives; why on earth would it? Positivity sells – they want your love, but don’t forget that in a sport bankrolled by businesses, the sponsors or partner cycling brands also want your money – not thorny stories lacking in digestibility.

That shift means the d-word is more likely to be further out of sight and mind, alongside the fact that it has been almost ten years since a seismic cycling scandal. It is easier than ever for doping, the sport’s number one enemy in the 21st century, to slide into the collective mental background.

The sport appears cleaner too. Empirically, there has been a fall in the number of positive doping tests, going from 29 in 2022 to 20 last year. It is over a decade since a rider was thrown off the Tour de France – Luca Paolini, for a cocaine positive in 2015.

Of course, most cycling fans are not naive. They know an apparent lull does not mean doping is a vanquished scourge. After all, it’s only been three weeks since Alberto Bruttomesso (Bahrain Victorious) was suspended for anti-doping rule violations.

Some modern sport fans' battlegrounds have also moved from doping doubt onto personality, beliefs or politics. In the polarised world of social media,where opinions fly around as freely as leaves in an autumn gale, I see both greater warmth and protectiveness towards some racers and a more deeply reinforced negativity against others.

Take Lidl-Trek rider Quinn Simmons, who told me in December 2025 for that certain people have "harassed" him his whole career, but that for every negative comment, he gets ten positive ones. Real life is very different to the online world's vocal, invisible minority: the American champion turned up to a 2026 Tour de France stage start in the town of Aurillac (i.e. the middle of nowhere) and encountered a French fan who had driven six hours to be there, wearing his team kit and impressively recreating his hair, beard and moustache combo.

Can Pogačar and today's peloton make reparations for previous errors?

Figurehead riders or squads tend to set the tone of every era, and Team Sky came to embody a lot of the previous era’s ills, as well as bringing a few of their own. Sharing Chris Froome's 2013 Tour power data with French newspaper – an act which is seemingly more than any leading contemporary team has done – did not quieten the questioning voices. The issue put forward remains the same as now: how do you prove a negative?

Ultimately, the zero tolerance team did not break the toxic cycle orcleanse themselves of the whiff of wrongdoing. In 2018, a British parliamentary committee found that the team "crossed an ethical line" over the use of medical exemptions for banned drugs, related to the jiffy bag farrago.

The drift away from traumatised scepticism has probably been helped by the changing of the guard: Sky is no longer the sponsor, and current incarnation Netcompany Ineos does not rule the roost.

After the transition of cycling power, new bosses UAE Team Emirates-XRG are not so different on the face of things. The probable richest team in the sport, winning Grand Tours repeatedly with a coterie of well-paid helpers, most of whom could be leaders in their own right – check, check and check again, straight from the "Death Star" playbook.

Associations with doping? They have a few. Mauro Gianetti and Matxin Fernández were managers of Saunier Duval, the team embroiled in doping scandals at the 2008 Tour de France. Kristijan Durasek was suspended after being named in Operation Aderlass in 2019, and rider Marc Soler's father Jaume received a (now overturned) suspension in February 2026 for working with banned ex-US Postal doctor Pepe Martí (there is no suggestion of wrongdoing by Marc Soler himself). Some fans may also look negatively upon the team's close association with the United Arab Emirates, a Middle East oil giant with a "dismal" human rights record, according to Amnesty International.

But none of this mud sticks, and that has much to do with the individual who defines this decade in pro cycling. Tadej Pogačar holds a lot of soft power, not just as an exemplar of spectacle and excellence, but as a transmitter of sympathetic feeling and good vibes to his team and the sport as a whole from his own actions and image.

To , if the modern peloton feels like repairmen for their predecessors' wrongdoings, Pogačar is the inadvertent head fixer in this move from embattled past to a present of fragile hope.

Though he has not faced the Spanish Inquisition level of questioning that Team Sky and its leaders encountered, Pogačar has quickly learned to answer challenging questions better than "I’ve never tested positive", his 2021 groan-worthy echo of a Lance Armstrong answer.

He has faced down queries about doping, his credibility and UAE's connections to the sport, never flying off the handle or pouring fuel on the fire like more combative superstars of recent generations. He understands that such inquiries are the lot of every new world-beater in this day and age "because cycling was so damaged in the past, before my time".

Generations change, but professional sport doesn't. Those seeking optimal performance will still use any legal method – such as carbon monoxide rebreathing, grubby but lawful – and some will inevitably go over the ethical and permissible line. Anti-doping agencies are historically under-funded and invariably playing catch-up against the next doping advances . It takes a long time for a culture to alter and, as a product of my time, scepticism is baked into me.

But I think some cycling fans have moved on, allowing themselves to be more cautiously hopeful – to believe again. That’s something to be cheerful about, with a caveat: after a good while without a sport-shaking controversy, the shock and damage will likely be even greater if an epochal racer is caught in the net. We aren’t out of the woods yet, just in a clearing.

title: 'He will restart as scheduled' – Egan Bernal more likely than ever to return for the 2027 season
author: Owen Rogers
text:
Former Tour de France and Giro d’Italia winner, Egan Bernal , is likely to return to the peloton in 2027 after some earlier doubts following the early closure of the Colombian rider’s season.

In that statement, Bernal said he intended to return in 2027, but left the door open to his premature departure from the sport, saying: "I don’t know exactly what the coming years hold, and I don’t think I need to know everything right now."

However, the 29-year-old recently travelled from his Colombian home to a team meeting at Netcompany’s Copenhagen headquarters, signalling his intention to continue racing. And if that wasn’t enough, comments from one of the team's sports directors, Dario Cioni, seem to have gone at least some way to confirming he will remain.

"Egan took a break from the season finale, but he had done the Giro and the Tour, so it’s not something we’ve never seen before," Cioni told .

"It’s clear that Bernal is a winner; he is not happy with finishing tenth. And rightly so, after the Giro and the Tour, he didn't feel he could be competitive, so he chose to end the season early. But he will restart as scheduled in 2027."

Winning the Tour de France at just 22, Bernal was heir apparent to the team’s Grand Tour-winning heritage. He went on to win the 2021 Giro d’Italia, but, despite some glimmers of hope, has never been the same since a career-threatening training crash in Colombia at the start of 2022.

The team gathering in Denmark was an opportunity for riders and staff to meet their new sponsor, Cioni, describing it as halfway between the end of the 2026 season and the start of 2027. Riders had medical checks, while staff had their chance for meetings.

In the interview with Cioni was also asked about the departure of Filippo Ganna to Lidl-Trek, a rider with whom he had worked closely.

"Those are choices in the hands of managers," Cioni said. "On a personal level, obviously I'm sorry, but these are team decisions that must be respected.

"A rider like Pippo [Ganna], who gives 100% towards the goals he sets for himself, pushes everyone to the limit. I think that as a team, until the arrival of Remco [Evenepoel], we were the point of reference in time trials.

"Beating Remco is not easy, but if we look at the collective, we are still at the forefront. We have the best package, certainly not inferior to Specialized, and we got to this point also thanks to a rider like Ganna."
